headline: Banned Nvidia B300 Servers Quoted at Up to $3.4 Million in Shenzhen
subheadline: A Washington Post dispatch found Huaqiangbei vendors openly quoting $3 million to $3.4 million for Nvidia's export-barred Blackwell B300 servers, with stock held in Hong Kong — though the Post could not verify the systems were genuine.
body:
• Sellers at Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei electronics market are quoting $3 million to $3.4 million for eight-GPU Nvidia Blackwell B300 servers, according to a Washington Post dispatch — up from about $2 million two months earlier.
  • The same server lists for about $600,000 in the United States, and the B300 has been barred from export to China by the U.S. Commerce Department since 2024.
  • Vendors told the Post their stock sits in warehouses in Hong Kong or elsewhere abroad, and said their buyers include customers in Russia and Iran as well as China.
  • The Post said it could not independently verify the authenticity of the B300 systems the vendors claimed to be selling.

At stalls inside Huaqiangbei, the sprawling electronics bazaar in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, sellers are openly quoting prices for Nvidia's most advanced artificial intelligence servers — hardware the U.S. Commerce Department has barred from export to China since 2024, according to a Washington Post dispatch reported this week.

The quotes are steep. An eight-GPU Nvidia Blackwell B300 system is being offered at $3 million to $3.4 million, the Post reported, up from roughly $2 million two months earlier. The same server lists for about $600,000 in the United States. Black-market prices for related restricted chips have also surged recently, according to the report.

Stock offshore, buyers beyond China

"Huaqiangbei moves everything from smartwatches and consumer drones to motherboards, and a "B300" label on a system offered at a market stall is not proof that genuine Blackwell hardware is inside."

Vendors told the Post that their stock does not sit in Shenzhen itself. It is held in warehouses in Hong Kong or elsewhere abroad, ready to move once a deal is agreed. One seller told the Post: "We plan to ship it to Hong Kong, with subsequent delivery directly to Russia or any other country by agreement." Others said they also sold to Russian and Iranian buyers — two other markets under U.S. export restrictions.

That supply route matters for enforcement. Export controls bind the sale and shipment of the chips, but a server held offshore and delivered through intermediaries is harder to trace than a direct shipment from a U.S. supplier, and the Huaqiangbei stalls function as storefronts rather than warehouses.

What is not verified

The Post was explicit about the limits of its own reporting: it could not independently verify the authenticity of the B300 systems the vendors claimed to sell. Huaqiangbei moves everything from smartwatches and consumer drones to motherboards, and a "B300" label on a system offered at a market stall is not proof that genuine Blackwell hardware is inside. The Videshi has not independently verified the vendors' claims either.

What is not in dispute is the policy backdrop. The U.S. Commerce Department maintains restrictions on exporting Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, a policy built on the argument that cutting-edge AI hardware is a national-security asset. A market in which the barred hardware is quoted openly — a few miles from where President Donald Trump recently met Chinese leader Xi Jinping, as the Post noted — states the enforcement problem in its plainest form.

Why it matters

For the technology industry, the report cuts in two directions. If genuine B300 systems are reaching Chinese buyers at scale, the controls are leaking at exactly the high end they were written to protect. If the offers are partly bluff — relabelled or lesser hardware sold at B300 prices — the surge in quoted prices still measures the premium that scarcity has created, and the risk that buyers and intermediaries are willing to carry.

Either way, the numbers vendors are quoting have moved sharply in two months, from about $2 million to as much as $3.4 million per system. That is the market's own reading of how tight the supply of restricted Nvidia hardware has become.

key_takeaways: Banned Nvidia B300 servers are quoted at $3M-$3.4M in Shenzhen, up from $2M two months prior.
The same server costs $600,000 in the U.S. and has been barred from export to China since 2024.
Vendors claim stock is held offshore in Hong Kong, with buyers in Russia, Iran, and China.
The authenticity of the B300 systems offered could not be independently verified by the Post.
The high prices reflect scarcity and the premium buyers are willing to pay for restricted AI hardware.
